title: Photons Are a Made‑Up Concept
content:
Abstract

The photon is widely treated in modern physics as a fundamental particle and the basic unit of electromagnetic radiation. This interpretation, rooted in early quantum theory, has shaped scientific understanding for more than a century. However, the photon concept introduces conceptual contradictions, including the idea of a massless particle behaving simultaneously as a wave and a particle, and the assumption that electromagnetic radiation is inherently quantized. This paper argues that the photon is not a physical entity but a mathematical abstraction created for convenience. Within the framework of Zot particles, electromagnetic radiation is understood as a continuous wave propagating through a sub‑elementary substrate. Light, therefore, is not composed of discrete packets but is a disturbance traveling through a medium, analogous to sound waves traveling through air. This perspective eliminates the paradoxes associated with photons and provides a more coherent foundation for understanding electromagnetic phenomena.

1. Introduction

The photon occupies a central place in modern physics. It is described as a massless particle, a quantum of the electromagnetic field, and the carrier of electromagnetic force. This hybrid concept emerged in the early 20th century as physicists attempted to reconcile classical wave theory with experimental observations that appeared to require quantization.

Despite its widespread acceptance, the photon concept raises several conceptual and philosophical issues. It is simultaneously treated as a particle and a wave, yet it lacks the defining characteristics of particles. It is said to have no mass, no size, and no internal structure, yet it is credited with transferring momentum and energy. These contradictions suggest that the photon may not be a physical object but a theoretical construct.

The purpose of this paper is to examine the photon critically and to present an alternative explanation grounded in the theory of Zot particles. According to this framework, electromagnetic radiation is not composed of particles but is a wave propagating through a sub‑elementary field. The photon, in this view, is a convenient abstraction rather than a physical entity.

2. The Standard Definition of a Photon

Physics textbooks and reference sources typically define the photon as:

  • an elementary particle,
  • a quantum of the electromagnetic field,
  • a massless boson,
  • always traveling at the speed of light in a vacuum,
  • responsible for electromagnetic interactions.

This definition attempts to merge classical and quantum descriptions by treating light as both a wave and a particle. The result is a hybrid model that is mathematically useful but conceptually ambiguous.

Several questions arise:

  • How can a particle have no mass, no size, and no internal structure?
  • How can something be both a wave and a particle simultaneously?
  • Why should electromagnetic radiation be quantized into discrete packets?
  • Why does the photon behave differently from all other particles?

These questions point to deeper issues in the photon model.

3. Conceptual Problems with the Photon Model

3.1. The Massless Particle Paradox

A photon is described as a particle with:

  • no mass,
  • no rest frame,
  • no internal components,
  • no spatial extent.

This makes it unlike any other particle in physics. The concept of a “particle” traditionally implies a localized object with definable properties. The photon violates this intuition.

3.2. Wave‑Particle Duality as a Conceptual Patch

Wave‑particle duality was introduced to reconcile contradictory observations. Instead of providing a physical explanation, it asserts that light behaves like a wave in some experiments and like a particle in others. This duality is not a physical mechanism but a conceptual compromise.

3.3. Quantization Does Not Require Particles

The quantization of energy in electromagnetic interactions arises from the properties of matter, not from the existence of discrete light particles. When atoms absorb or emit energy in discrete amounts, the mathematics naturally produces quantized values. This does not imply that light itself is composed of discrete packets.

3.4. The Measurement Problem

The photon model relies heavily on the observer’s measurement apparatus. Whether light appears particle‑like or wave‑like depends on the experimental setup. This suggests that the photon is a description of measurement outcomes, not a description of physical reality.

4. Light as a Wave

4.1. The Zot Particle Framework

The theory of Zot particles proposes that the universe is permeated by a dense substrate composed of sub‑elementary units. All fields, including the electromagnetic field, arise from the collective behavior of these units. The substrate behaves like a medium, though not in the classical mechanical sense.

4.2. Light as a Continuous Wave

In this framework:

  • Light is a wave traveling through the Zot substrate.
  • The substrate supports oscillations across a wide range of frequencies.
  • The wave is continuous, not composed of discrete packets.
  • Biological systems detect specific frequency ranges based on their structure.

Our eyes are tuned to detect a narrow band of these frequencies, just as our ears detect a narrow band of sound frequencies.

4.3. Why the Photon Is Unnecessary

If light is a wave propagating through a medium, then:

  • There is no need for a massless particle.
  • Energy transfer can be explained through wave‑matter interactions.
  • Quantization arises from the structure of matter, not from the structure of light.
  • The paradoxes of wave‑particle duality disappear.

The photon becomes an unnecessary conceptual layer.

5. The Sound‑Wave Analogy

The photon model is equivalent to claiming that sound travels as discrete packets of “sound particles.” This would be absurd, because:

  • Sound is a pressure wave in air.
  • It propagates through the collective motion of molecules.
  • There is no need to invent a “sound particle” to explain it.

Similarly, light is a disturbance in the Zot substrate. Treating it as a particle complicates the explanation without adding clarity.

6. Historical Reasons for the Photon Concept

6.1. Early Quantum Theory

The photon concept emerged during a period when physicists were attempting to explain:

  • the photoelectric effect,
  • blackbody radiation,
  • atomic emission spectra.

Quantization appeared necessary to match experimental results.

6.2. Mathematical Convenience

The photon simplifies calculations involving:

  • energy exchange,
  • momentum transfer,
  • emission and absorption processes.

However, mathematical convenience does not imply physical reality.

6.3. Influence of Einstein and Early Quantum Pioneers

Einstein’s interpretation of light quanta strongly influenced the development of quantum theory. His authority helped solidify the photon concept, even though alternative interpretations were possible.

7. A Sub‑Elementary Interpretation of Electromagnetic Radiation

7.1. Waves Without Particles

In the Zot framework, electromagnetic radiation is:

  • a continuous wave,
  • a collective oscillation of the substrate,
  • capable of carrying energy and information,
  • not composed of discrete units.

7.2. Interaction With Matter

When light interacts with matter:

  • atoms absorb energy in discrete amounts,
  • the substrate wave transfers energy continuously,
  • quantization arises from atomic structure, not from the wave itself.


7.3. Eliminating Wave‑Particle Duality

If light is purely a wave, then:

  • there is no duality,
  • no paradox,
  • no need for a particle interpretation.

This restores conceptual clarity.

8. Implications for Physics

8.1. Rethinking Electromagnetic Theory

The Zot‑wave interpretation suggests that:

  • the electromagnetic field is a manifestation of substrate dynamics,
  • Maxwell’s equations describe large‑scale behavior,
  • quantum effects arise from matter, not from light.

8.2. Revisiting Quantum Optics

Many quantum optical phenomena can be reinterpreted as:

  • wave interference,
  • wave‑matter coupling,
  • quantized absorption and emission.

8.3. Unifying Fields and Forces

The Zot substrate provides a common foundation for:

  • electromagnetic waves,
  • gravitational waves,
  • matter waves,
  • biological signaling waves.


9. Conclusion

The photon, as traditionally defined, is a conceptual construct rather than a physical entity. It was introduced to simplify the mathematics of early quantum theory, but it introduces paradoxes that are unnecessary within the Zot particle framework. Light is more coherently understood as a wave propagating through a sub‑elementary substrate, analogous to sound traveling through air. This perspective eliminates the need for massless particles and provides a clearer foundation for understanding electromagnetic phenomena.
